prompt.context:
Our client is a fabric producer called To-Dye-For Fabrics. The company purchases fabric in bulk from overseas and then dyes batches of fabric in colors ordered by clients. It produces 1.4 million square meters of product each month and its average variable cost is $0.60 per square meter.

Processed batches have the following distribution:
- 40% of the batches are greater than 5,000 square meters
- 30% of the batches are between 3,000 and 5,000 square meters
- 30% of the batches are less than 3,000 square meters

To-Dye-For uses two different processes to dye its fabrics:
Continuous Dyeing: where washing and dyeing are integrated in a continuous process. This process is used for 70% of the company's production and is cheaper for batches of over 5,000 square meters.
Batch Processing: in which the washing and dyeing machines are independent. The machines in this line need to be set up prior to each batch being processed. Batch processing is used with the remaining production and is cheaper for batches under 5,000 square meters.
If a batch has to be processed using a more expensive process, the cost is $0.05 per square meter.
prompt.question: Our client has asked us to recommend how it might reduce its total costs. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: How frequently do clients place orders and how quickly are they fulfilled?
clarifying_info.a: Clients usually make one or two orders during a month. Those orders are aggregated and usually fulfilled within 15 days.

clarifying_info.q: Is the 15-day fill time critical to customers?
clarifying_info.a: The 15-day fill time is not crucial to customers — they are okay with having orders filled within a month.

clarifying_info.q: What is the set-up time for the Batch process machine and what is its installed capacity?
clarifying_info.a: The set-up time for the Batch process machine is one hour and the installed capacity for that process is 700,000 square meters/month (assuming no set-up downtime).

framework: Identify how production volume is currently split across batch sizes
Map which process (Continuous Dyeing vs. Batch Processing) is used for each batch-size tier
Calculate the volume being processed by the wrong (more expensive) process and quantify the over-cost
Determine why the mismatch exists — examine Batch Processing capacity including set-up downtime
Develop recommendations to eliminate the mismatch: (a) add capacity, (b) aggregate orders into larger batches
Quantify the savings and, if additional investment is proposed, calculate the maximum justifiable price

questions.prompt: How is the 1.4 million m2 of monthly production currently split by batch size, and which process is used for each tier?
questions.guidance: Continuous Dyeing handles 70% of production = 980,000 m2. Batch Processing handles 30% = 420,000 m2. By batch-size distribution: <3,000 m2 = 420,000 m2; 3,000–5,000 m2 = 420,000 m2; >5,000 m2 = 560,000 m2. Only batches >5,000 m2 (560,000 m2) should use Continuous Dyeing cheaply; batches ≤5,000 m2 (840,000 m2) should use Batch Processing. The candidate should identify that 980,000 m2 goes through Continuous Dyeing but only 560,000 m2 should — so 420,000 m2 is being over-processed at the more expensive rate.

math.setup: Total production = 1,400,000 m2/month. Continuous Dyeing = 70% x 1,400,000. Batch Processing = 30% x 1,400,000.
steps: Volume that should use Continuous Dyeing (>5,000 m2): 0.40 x 1,400,000 = 560,000 m2
Volume incorrectly using Continuous Dyeing: 980,000 - 560,000 = 420,000 m2

questions.prompt: Why are Batch Processing machines not absorbing the smaller batches that should go through them?
questions.guidance: Batch Processing installed capacity is 700,000 m2/month assuming no set-up downtime. Actual throughput is only 420,000 m2/month. The machine produces only 420,000/700,000 = 60% of the time; the remaining 40% is consumed by set-up. This means the machine is at effective full utilisation and cannot take on the additional 420,000 m2 that should ideally move off Continuous Dyeing.

math.setup: Installed capacity = 700,000 m2/month. Actual production = 420,000 m2/month.
math.answer: The Batch Processing machine runs at 60% productive time; 40% is set-up downtime — it is effectively at capacity and cannot absorb more volume.

questions.prompt: If the client buys a second Batch Process machine to eliminate the over-cost, what is the maximum price it should pay? (Discount rate = 10%)
questions.guidance: The savings from eliminating the over-cost are $21,000/month = $252,000/year. Treating the machine as having perpetual life and using the perpetuity formula: Maximum price = Annual savings / discount rate. The candidate should arrive at $2,520,000.

math.setup: Annual savings = $21,000 x 12. Discount rate = 10%. Maximum price = Annual savings / discount rate (perpetuity).
math.answer: $2,520,000 is the maximum price to pay for the new Batch Process machine.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond buying a new machine, what other options exist to reduce the over-cost or create larger batches?

categories.name: Order aggregation
ideas: Aggregate client orders over a longer window (up to one month) to form larger batches above 5,000 m2
Combine orders from multiple clients for the same colour or fabric type into a single large batch

categories.name: Commercial and planning integration
ideas: Integrate production planning processes with clients so orders can be timed and sized to hit efficient batch thresholds
Train the sales force to encourage clients to consolidate orders and place fewer, larger orders

categories.name: Incentive design
ideas: Offer pricing incentives to clients who place larger or less frequent orders
Design incentives for the sales force tied to order size or batch efficiency rather than order count

categories.name: Process optimisation
ideas: Reduce Batch Processing set-up time to increase effective capacity without capital expenditure
Re-sequence batches to minimise colour changeovers and reduce total set-up events

recommendation: The root cause is a process-volume mismatch: 420,000 m2/month of small-batch fabric is being processed via Continuous Dyeing at an unnecessary $0.05/m2 premium, costing $21,000/month, because Batch Processing capacity is fully consumed by set-up downtime.

Primary recommendation: Aggregate client orders to a monthly cycle (customers are comfortable with up to one month fulfillment), which allows smaller orders to be combined into batches above 5,000 m2 and processed on the already-cheaper Continuous Dyeing line — eliminating the over-cost without capital investment.

Secondary recommendation: If aggregation alone is insufficient, purchase one additional Batch Processing machine (maximum justifiable price: $2,520,000 at a 10% discount rate) to absorb the 420,000 m2 currently misrouted to Continuous Dyeing.
risks: Customers may resist any change to current fulfillment timing even if they say they are comfortable with a monthly window
Aggregating orders by colour/type may be operationally complex and could increase coordination overhead
A second machine adds fixed cost; if production volume declines, the savings may not materialise
next_steps: Conduct detailed customer interviews to confirm willingness to accept monthly order cycles
Model the order mix to determine how much volume can realistically be aggregated above 5,000 m2 before committing to new capital
Investigate set-up time reduction initiatives (lean/SMED) as a lower-cost path to freeing Batch Processing capacity
Develop sales force training and incentive programme around order consolidation
